newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian parliament faces vote on child sex report.
newsitem.headline: Belgian parliament faces vote on child sex report.

text.p: The Belgian parliament faces a test of moral courage on Friday, with a key vote on a report by a special commission that exposed shambolic investigations into the national scandal of child kidnappings, rapes and murders.

The report by a cross-party parliamentary commission, published on Tuesday, spared noone in its scathing description of rivalry between the country's three police forces and lackadaisical magistrates.
Among other things it wants to bring all the police forces into a unified structure and for a thorough reform of the system of public prosecutors and magistrates.
Both of these proposals have important ramifications because they are part of the system through which the various political parties in Belgium exercise their influence at local level.
Five young girls have been found dead since August, and police are still looking for other missing children. Two convicted child molesters have been charged with murder.

But the report, which followed six months of often televised hearings, suggested that sheer incompetence might not have been the sole explanation for the failure of investigators to find or rescue the children. The perpetrators might have had protection.
The report, which put forward a series of reform proposals, was agreed unanimously by the commission.
The crucial question facing the parliament on Friday -- and one that the Belgian public will be watching closely -- will be whether party politics can again be kept at bay.

"I hope that we will be able to adopt this report unanimously tomorrow," Patrick Dewael, a member of the commission and of the VLD Flemish Liberal opposition said during a parliamentary debate on Thursday.
"This is an important moment for democracy," Didier Reynders of the PRL Francophone Liberal opposition said.
"There must be no majority versus opposition in the parliamentary debates (on the reforms). These must be true debates," he added.

In October more than 250,000 people marched through Brussels in sympathy with the victims and their parents, but also as a show of disgust at a system seen by most as being incompetent and by some as being corrupt.

Intrusion of party politics into the vote on the report and, even more, on the debates in coming months on the proposed reforms would risk bringing an even bigger and much angrier mob onto the streets.

"What our people want...is the truth so that these events can never be repeated," said Patrick Moriau, a member of the PS Francophone Socialist Party who was forced to quit the commission over allegations he knew of bribes allegedly paid to the party in the late 1980s by French aerospace firm Dassault.
The government has promised a review of the early release of sex offenders as well as proposing that a magistrate is immediately appointed to the case when a child goes missing.

It has also pledged to abolish the political promotion of magistrates, more clearly define the tasks of the different police forces, promote the rights of victims and to set up a special centre for missing children.
The commission will carry on working until September 30 on its hypothesis that the criminals exposed so far may have had high level protection -- a view held by many people.
